notes.meaning: Zechariah looks up and sees a vision of a man holding a measuring line. Measuring shows that God is carefully planning the future rebuilding and expansion of Jerusalem. Many older writers understand this measuring figure to be the Messiah Himself, directing the restoration of His people.

Zechariah asks the man where he is going, and the man replies that he is going to measure the length and width of Jerusalem. At that time, the city still lay in ruins with very few people living inside it. Taking its measurements was God's way of promising that Jerusalem would be rebuilt and made ready for a full population.

The angel who had been explaining the visions to Zechariah leaves, and another angel steps out to meet him. This second messenger brings an urgent message directly from the Lord. God sends His heavenly messengers swiftly to bring direction and comfort to His servants.

The second angel commands the first to run and deliver good news to the young prophet Zechariah. Jerusalem will become so filled with people and livestock that it cannot be contained within stone walls, spreading out like open country towns. God promised that the future community would grow far larger than the ancient city had ever been.

differ.view: Reformed teachers often understand the unwalled city as a picture of the church of Christ expanding throughout the world without physical borders.
Some evangelicals see this being fulfilled in the physical growth of modern Jerusalem beyond its old walls and in the future earthly reign of the Messiah.

notes.meaning: The Lord promises that Jerusalem will not need stone walls for defense because He Himself will surround it like a wall of fire. He also promises to be the glorious presence dwelling within the city. Just as God guarded Israel with a pillar of fire in the wilderness, His presence is the true protection and glory of His people.

The Lord calls out with an urgent cry for the Jewish exiles to flee from Babylon in the north and hurry home. God had scattered them in judgment across the earth like the four winds, but now He is gathering them back. When God opens the way to freedom, His people are urged not to stay comfortably settled in a land of exile.

God calls on the people of Zion who are still living in Babylon to break free and escape. Many exiles had grown comfortable in captivity and were slow to make the hard journey back to Jerusalem. God urges them to leave that pagan society behind so they will not be caught up in the judgment coming upon it.

The Lord of Hosts announces that He is sending His messenger against the nations that plundered His people. God declares that whoever harms His people touches the apple—the pupil—of His own eye, which is the most tender and carefully guarded part of the body. This image shows God's deep affection for His chosen people and how swiftly He will act to defend them.

The Lord says that with a simple wave of His hand, He will strike down the hostile nations and turn them into plunder for their former servants. A single gesture of divine power is enough to bring down mighty empires. When this deliverance happens, the people will have proof that the Lord of Hosts truly sent His messenger.

The people of Jerusalem, called the daughter of Zion, are urged to sing and rejoice because the Lord Himself is coming to dwell in their midst. His arrival brings salvation from enemies and restores close fellowship with His people. Christians understand this promise as fulfilled first in the coming of Jesus Christ in human flesh, and fully at His final return.

On that day, many Gentile nations will turn to the Lord and be joined to Him as His covenant people alongside Israel. God repeats His promise to dwell among them, showing that His grace reaches people from all backgrounds. The speaker is described both as the Lord and as someone sent by the Lord of Hosts, pointing to the divine Son sent by the Father.

differ.view: Reformed Christians understand this promise as being fulfilled in the Christian church, where Gentile nations are joined to God through faith in Christ.
Some evangelicals believe this will be literally fulfilled during an earthly thousand-year reign of Christ after His second coming.

notes.meaning: The Lord promises to claim Judah as His special possession in the Holy Land and to choose Jerusalem once again. Even though they had suffered through the exile, God's covenant with His people was never canceled. This verse contains the only place in the Bible that uses the exact phrase "the Holy Land," made holy because God chooses to dwell there.

All humanity is summoned to fall silent in reverence and awe before the Lord. God has roused Himself from His holy dwelling in heaven and is actively moving to save His people and judge the nations. When God arises to carry out His plans, human beings can only stand in quiet submission and trust His power.
